title: Fit for you
hook: judge every word and act that fits you, and don't be swayed by blame (Meditations 5.3)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was galene, the calm of a sea gone flat. Your line was a sea gone flat.

There's always someone with notes. You start eating differently and a relative comments. You speak up at a meeting and someone rolls their eyes. You give money to a cause and a friend calls it naive. Sometimes the critic is right, and it's worth listening. But often the right thing simply comes with a small crowd of people who'd rather you didn't. Marcus Aurelius, whose every public act had an audience, gave himself a rule for that crowd.
screen: `THERE'S ALWAYS SOMEONE WITH NOTES.` → `THE RIGHT THING HAS CRITICS.` → `FIT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Judge every word and act that is in line with nature, Marcus writes in book five, entry three, as fit for you. In Stoic terms, in line with nature means in line with what a reasoning, social creature is made for: honest, fair, useful to others. That's the test, and it comes first. Then: don't let the blame or the talk of certain people that follows turn you aside. If a thing is good to do or say, don't think it beneath you. Notice the order. Test the act first. If it passes, the critics don't get a vote. Those people, he says, have their own ruling mind and follow their own impulses. Don't keep looking over at them. That isn't contempt. Their mind is theirs to steer, and yours is yours. Go straight on, he finishes, following your own nature and the common nature, because the road of both is one. What's right for you, done honestly, is also right for the whole. This doesn't mean ignore all feedback. Elsewhere Marcus asks to be corrected, gladly, when he's wrong. A critic with a reason gets heard, and maybe changes your mind. A critic with only disapproval doesn't get to decide what's fit for you.
screen: `JUDGE EACH ACT AS FIT FOR YOU.` · `DON'T LET THE BLAME TURN YOU ASIDE.` · `THEY HAVE THEIR OWN RULING MIND.` · `ONE STRAIGHT ROAD.` · then, large: `FIT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Think of one right thing you've held back from because of a critic, real or imagined, and test it honestly: is it fair, true, useful? If it fails, let it go. If it passes, let the critic keep their own mind, and picture yourself doing it calmly, without needing to win them over.
Marcus, who said to judge every word and act in line with nature as fit for you, and not let the blame of critics turn you aside. Today's word.
Your line: fit for me. Test the act first; then the critics don't get a vote. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use Meditations 5.3 in two steps: first test an act for fairness and honesty, then, if it passes, don't let disapproval alone turn them aside.

notes: 5.3 paraphrased: judge every word and deed in accordance with nature to be fit for you; don't be diverted by the blame which follows from any people, nor by their words; if a thing is good to be done or said, don't consider it unworthy of you; those persons have their own ruling faculty and follow their own movement; don't regard them, but go straight on, following your own nature and the common nature, for the way of both is one. Confirm.
6.21: if anyone can show me that I do not think or act rightly, I will gladly change. Cited for 'asks to be corrected, gladly'. Confirm.
'Criticized for a living' is light shorthand for an emperor's public life; confirm tone.
